previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, neurogenic bladder, and bilateral below-knee amputations was readmitted one day after discharge due to fever and hypotension. She was diagnosed with sepsis likely from a urinary tract infection caused by pan-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae. She was treated with intravenous meropenem for seven days and improved clinically with resolution of fever and normalization of labs. Her acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia resolved with fluid resuscitation and holding lisinopril. Blood and urine cultures eventually cleared. She was restarted on home medications including metoprolol, lisinopril, and gabapentin. Urology planned outpatient training in clean intermittent catheterization to reduce future UTIs. She was discharged home with nursing services, stable and afebrile, with follow-up arranged in urology, infectious disease, and primary care.

Discharge Instructions:
It was a pleasure providing care for you during your 
hospitalizations. 

You were admitted for an infection in your urine and blood. You 
were treated with antibiotics through your veins. There was 
concern that you might have a rectovaginal fistula (a small 
tract connecting the rectum to the vagina). Rectovaginal 
fistuals can occasionaly increase your risk of getting recurrent 
urinary tract infections which is why it is very important to 
work it up. Colorectal surgery, gynecology and urology 
specialists were all consulted and performed a workup to see if 
you had the fistula. The images we took of your pelvis did not 
show any obvious fistula. You will continue to get this worked 
up with Dr. ___ surgery) outpatient.

While you were in the hospital, your diabetes was managed by 
specialists. They adjusted your insulin regimen to make sure 
your sugars were in a good range.

The following changes were made to your medications:
You metoprolol and lisinopril were initially held because your 
blood pressure was very low when you first came into the 
hospital. They were then added back when your blood pressure 
increased.
Your insulin sliding scale was adjusted. You were given 4 of 
glargine a day, instead of your prior 6 a day.
Your gabapentin dose was adjusted.
You were given antibiotics through your veins. You will continue 
some of these antibiotics when you leave the hospital.

Please resume all of your home medications after you leave the 
hospital. Please resume self-catheterization as well. You can 
follow up with urologists to help you do this. 
Self-cetheterization can minimize urinary tract infections.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ female with hypertension.

STUDY:  Portable AP upright chest radiograph.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  An IVC filter is noted in the inferior aspect of the image.  The
heart size is normal allowing for technique.  Mediastinal contour appears
normal.  In the right upper lung, there persists a steak-like opacity
concerning for persisting infection.  Additionally, in the retrocardiac
region, there is increased opacity which may represent atelectasis or
scarring, although an underlying infectious process cannot be ruled out. 
Blunting of the right costophrenic angle suggests a small pleural effusion. 
There is no pneumothorax and the osseous structures appear intact.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Right upper lung steak-like opacity concerning for infection.
2.  Retrocardiac opacity may represent atelectasis or scarring, although
underlying infectious process cannot be excluded.
3.  Trace right pleural effusion.

INDICATION:  ___ with type 1 diabetes, recurrent UTIs, urosepsis and
question of rectovaginal fistula and bladder urethral conduit.

COMPARISON:  Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector helical scanning of the pelvis was performed prior
to and following the administration of rectal contrast.  Coronal and sagittal
reformats were displayed.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH RECTAL CONTRAST:   Contrast is seen within the rectum
and decompressed sigmoid colon with no evidence of extravasation or
fistulization to the vagina or bladder. The rectum is only partially
distended, which could somewhat limit evaluation.  Air is seen within the
vagina, a finding that is commonly seen and nonspecific. Foley catheter and
air are seen within the bladder (air is not specific in the presence of a
Foley). Delineation of soft tissues in the pelvis is limited by noncontrast
technique.   The pelvic small bowel loops appear normal.  The appendix,
adjacent to the sigmoid colon (4:35), is gas-filled and normal in caliber.

There is extensive stranding and fluid within the right paracolic gutter
adjacent to the ascending colon, concerning for colitis.  The stranding and
fluid appear separate from the right kidney and pancreas, making inflammatory
processes of those organs less likely.

Infrarenal IVC filter is in place.  Multiple linear calcifications in both
kidneys are consistent with vascular calcifications.  There is a 3-mm calculus
within the interpolar region of the right kidney, unchanged from ___.  There are also multiple calculi within the gall bladder, with no
evidence of cholecystitis.  Extensive atherosclerotic calcification within the
abdominal aortoiliac vessels and femoral vessels is unchanged.

No bone findings of malignancy.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No demonstration of rectovaginal or rectovesicular fistula.  Evaluation is
somewhat limited due to lack of complete distention of the rectum, and if
there is continued clinical concern for rectovaginal fistula, a pelvic MRI
could be obtained. Fluoroscopic examination could also be performed if MRI is
unrevealing.

2.  Extensive fluid and stranding surrounding the right ascending colon,
concerning for colitis which may be infectious, inflammatory or ischemic in
etiology.

3.  Unchanged non-obstructing 3-mm right renal calculus.

4.  Cholelithiasis.

Results discussed via telephone with resident caring for the patient on
___.

SINGLE AP PORTABLE VIEW OF THE CHEST

REASON FOR EXAM:  Assess line.

Left IJ catheter tip is at the cavoatrial junction.  There is no pneumothorax.
Small bilateral pleural effusions right greater than left have increased with
increasing bibasilar opacities left greater than right.  These opacities are
likely atelectasis but superimposed infection cannot be totally excluded. 
Right upper lobe opacities are persistent from ___.  There is no
pneumothorax.

EXAM:  CT abdomen ___.

COMPARISON:  CT pelvis ___.

CLINICAL INFORMATION:  A ___ female with question of rectovaginal
fistula.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial images were acquired of the abdomen and pelvis following the
administration of rectal contrast, and p.o. contrast.  Images were reformatted
in the coronal and sagittal planes.

FINDINGS:

LUNG BASES:  There is increase in bilateral pleural effusions, moderate on the
right, small on the left compared with prior.  There is associated bibasilar
atelectasis.  Again seen is linear atelectasis or scar in the bilateral lung
bases.

ABDOMEN:  Evaluation of the abdomen is limited by lack of iodinated
intravenous contrast; however, within these limitations, the liver, spleen,
and adrenal glands appear normal.  The gallbladder contains dense material
consistent with stones or sludge.  The pancreas is diminutive in size.  The
distal esophagus, stomach, and duodenum appear normal.  The kidneys contain a
punctate calcification within the right mid pole, and arterial calcification. 
There is nonspecific minimal stranding around the bilateral kidneys.  There is
no hydronephrosis.  An IVC filter is seen within the IVC.  The aorta is
calcified but normal in caliber.

PELVIS:  Positive contrast is seen within the rectum.  No contrast material is
seen within the vagina to suggest rectovaginal fistula.  The bladder contains
a Foley catheter and air, and is otherwise unremarkable.  The colon is filled
with positive contrast material, and is otherwise unremarkable.  The appendix
appears normal.

BONES:  No concerning osseous lesions are seen.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence of rectovaginal fistula.

2.  Interval increase in size of bilateral pleural effusions.

INDICATION:  New PICC 41 cm.  Evaluate for tip placement.

COMPARISON:  ___.

AP UPRIGHT RADIOGRAPH OF THE CHEST:  Right PICC is terminating in the distal
SVC.  Left IJ is terminating at the cavoatrial junction.  Interval improvement
in parenchymal aeration with persistent right upper lobe linear opacity likely
correspond to region of scarring and bronchiectasis seen on CT from ___. Moderate cardiomegaly is stable.  Pulmonary vascularity is normal as are
the hilar contours.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Right PICC in distal SVC, standard location.
2.  Improving parenchymal aeration with residual right upper lobe scarring and
bronchiectasis.
